edges.mechanism: Higher soil organic carbon increases aggregate stability and micropore formation, allowing soil to retain more plant-available water.
Greater organic-carbon inputs provide diverse substrates and microsites that support a larger and more diverse soil microbial community.
Organic matter promotes stable soil aggregates and biological pore formation, increasing the rate at which water enters and moves through soil.
Greater soil water storage maintains plant-available water for longer during periods of rainfall deficit.
Higher infiltration transfers a greater fraction of rainfall below the soil surface, increasing the water available for aquifer recharge where geological conditions permit.
Greater infiltration reduces rapid surface runoff and allows soils to retain or transform some sediments and dissolved pollutants before water reaches streams.
Diverse microbial communities support decomposition and nutrient transformations that can reduce concentrations of some organic pollutants and reactive nutrients.
Greater drought resilience maintains vegetation productivity and habitat resources during water stress, reducing drought-driven local species losses.
Trees add carbon to soil through litterfall, root turnover and rhizodeposition, increasing soil organic-carbon inputs.
Tree litter and root-derived organic matter improve soil structure while canopy cover reduces direct soil evaporation and temperature extremes.
Tree roots create macropores and litter protects soil aggregates, allowing rainfall to infiltrate rather than becoming surface runoff.

Improved soil structure and infiltration under suitable forest conditions can increase the fraction of rainfall entering subsurface flow pathways, although tree water use can offset recharge in some settings.
Trees and associated understory vegetation provide nesting sites, shelter and seasonal floral resources that can support pollinator populations.
Greater tree cover creates additional vertical vegetation structure and habitat niches that can support more species.
Continuous tree cover can connect otherwise isolated habitat patches and provide movement corridors for forest-associated organisms.
Different crops provide distinct root exudates, residues and rooting patterns, creating a wider range of microbial substrates and niches.
A diversity of crops can extend the timing and variety of floral resources and increase habitat heterogeneity available to pollinators.
Crop diversification creates more varied habitat structure and resource conditions than continuous monoculture, supporting a broader range of associated organisms.
Crop rotation and diversification can interrupt host-specific pest cycles and reduce dependence on repeated broad-spectrum pesticide applications.
Increasing fragmentation separates habitat patches and increases gaps between them, reducing the continuity of suitable movement pathways.
Fragmentation reduces available habitat area and isolates populations, increasing local extinction risk and limiting recolonization.
Fragmented landscapes reduce the availability and continuity of nesting and floral resources, increasing movement costs for pollinators.
Connected habitats facilitate dispersal, recolonization and gene flow, allowing more species to persist across the landscape.
Connected flowering and nesting habitats reduce movement barriers and improve access to complementary resources needed throughout pollinator life cycles.
Pesticide exposure can cause direct mortality, behavioral impairment and reduced reproduction in pollinators, with effects depending on compound and exposure.
Broad-spectrum pesticide exposure can reduce populations of non-target organisms and simplify food webs, lowering the number of species able to persist.
Pesticides transported by runoff, erosion and drainage can increase toxic contaminant concentrations in surface waters.
Excess nitrogen and phosphorus escaping fields through runoff and leaching can cause eutrophication, oxygen depletion and elevated nitrate concentrations in water.
Excess nutrient enrichment can favor a small number of fast-growing species and reduce light or habitat availability for nutrient-sensitive species.
Lower concentrations of toxic contaminants and excess nutrients maintain oxygen availability and physiological conditions suitable for a wider range of aquatic and riparian species.
